questions.prompt: Mounts: /data (named volume) and /cfg (read-only bind mount). The program writes /data/out.csv, /cfg/new.yaml and /var/tmp/x. Which write fails?
options: /data/out.csv, because a named volume is read-only inside a container
None of them, since every path accepts writes while the container runs
/cfg/new.yaml (read-only mount)
/var/tmp/x, because the container's root filesystem is read-only
questions.explanation: A read-only mount rejects writes; the others succeed.

questions.prompt: Mounts: /results (volume) only. The program writes 5 files: 3 under /results, 1 under /tmp, 1 under /root/.cache. After docker rm, how many survive? (integer, tolerance 0.5)
questions.explanation: Only the 3 under the mounted volume.

questions.prompt: The mount target is /results but the program writes to /result/run.json (typo). What is the consequence?
options: The write fails immediately, because the directory /result does not exist
Docker creates a new volume called /result and keeps the file there
The file lands in the writable layer and is lost on docker rm
The file is written to the volume anyway, because Docker fixes the typo
questions.explanation: /result is not covered by the mount, so it goes to the container layer silently.

questions.prompt: Mounts /results (volume) and /results/cache (bind mount). Where does /results/cache/model.bin go?
options: The bind mount (longest matching target)
The writable layer, because nested mounts are not allowed to overlap
Both the volume and the bind mount, since a write goes to every mount
The volume, because it was declared first and so takes priority
questions.explanation: The most specific (longest) target covering the path wins.

questions.prompt: A 7-instruction Dockerfile has the code COPY as instruction 3 and the dependency install as instruction 4. After editing code, how many instructions are reused from cache? (integer, tolerance 0.5)
questions.explanation: Instructions 1 and 2 are unchanged; 3 and all following are rebuilt.

questions.prompt: After reordering so that the lock COPY is instruction 3, the install is 4 and the code COPY is 5 (7 instructions in total), how many instructions are reused after a code edit? (integer, tolerance 0.5)
Five images share 200 MB of base layers and add 10 MB each. Storage with sharing? (integer MB, tolerance 0.5)
Which is a bad practice in a Dockerfile for a reproducible experiment?
options: COPY of the lock file before the code
FROM python:3.12-slim pinned, secrets passed at run time
A .dockerignore excluding .git and .env
FROM python:latest and ENV API_KEY=... baked into the image
questions.explanation: An unpinned base changes over time and secrets in ENV are readable from the image.

questions.prompt: Files written by a root container into a bind-mounted host folder cannot be deleted by you. What is the standard fix?
options: Switch to the latest image, which no longer runs as root
Remove the volume so that the files are not kept after the run
Run the container with --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"
Use sudo for every file operation on the host from now on
questions.explanation: The process then writes files owned by your uid.

questions.prompt: A container is stopped (not removed). You start it again. What is true of its writable layer?
options: It was moved into a volume when the container stopped, so it persists
It still exists with its files, because only docker rm discards it
It was moved into the image when the container stopped, as a new layer
It was discarded when the container stopped, so the files are gone
questions.explanation: Stopping keeps the container and its writable layer; removing deletes it.

questions.prompt: Your teammate's results vanished after they updated the image and recreated the container. Explain the likely cause and give the corrected run command.
rubric: Results were written to the container filesystem (or an unmounted path), which is discarded on recreation.
Fix: mount a named volume or bind mount at the results path, e.g. -v results:/results, and write there.
Verify with ls in a second container and record the image digest with the results.

questions.prompt: A Dockerfile has two independent rebuild steps in this order: step A costs 100 s and changes in 2% of commits, step B costs 10 s and changes in 50% of commits. A step is rebuilt if it or any earlier step changed. What is the expected build time per commit in seconds? (tolerance 0.1)
questions.explanation: Step A is rebuilt with probability 0.02, costing 100 x 0.02 = 2 s. Step B is rebuilt if A or B changed: 1 - (0.98)(0.5) = 0.51, costing 10 x 0.51 = 5.1 s. Total 2 + 5.1 = 7.1 s. For comparison, the order B, A gives 10 x 0.5 + 100 x (1 - 0.5 x 0.98) = 5 + 51 = 56 s, which agrees with the exchange rule: c(1-q)/q is 4900 for A and 10 for B, so A should come first.

questions.prompt: Images X = A|B|C and Y = A|B'|C are built, where layer C is a byte-identical changeset in both but B and B' differ. Using the OCI ChainID definition, which statement is correct?
options: The two C layers share one stored copy, because their DiffIDs are equal and a layer store is keyed by DiffID.
Only layer A is shared by ChainID; the two C layers have equal DiffIDs but different ChainIDs, so a ChainID-keyed store holds them separately.
No layer at all is shared, because the ChainID of the base layer A also changes when B' replaces B above it, so the whole stack differs.
The two C layers are shared, because ChainID(C) is defined as the digest of its DiffID alone and ignores the layers beneath.
questions.explanation: ChainID(A) = DiffID(A) is the same in both images. ChainID(A|B) = Digest(ChainID(A) + ' ' + DiffID(B)) differs from ChainID(A|B') because the DiffIDs differ, and ChainID(A|B|C) = Digest(ChainID(A|B) + ' ' + DiffID(C)) inherits that difference even though DiffID(C) is the same. So A is shared and the C layers are not. Option 0 confuses DiffID (changeset identity) with ChainID (identity of the resulting filesystem); option 2 forgets that a hash chain depends only on layers below; option 3 describes the single-layer base case only.

questions.prompt: A Dockerfile does COPY dataset.tar /data/ (2 GB), then RUN tar -xf /data/dataset.tar -C /data (6 GB extracted), then RUN rm /data/dataset.tar. Compute the image size added by these three instructions, explain why the last one does not help, and give two ways to fix it.
rubric: Size is 2 + 6 + ~0 = 8 GB: layers are immutable changesets, and the rm layer holds only a whiteout (.wh.dataset.tar) of about zero bytes, so the 2 GB tarball stays in the earlier layer.
The deleted file is still pushed, pulled and readable by anyone who extracts that layer; the whiteout only hides it when layers are stacked.
Fix 1: never put the tarball in a layer, for example RUN curl ... | tar -x in one instruction, or create and delete within a single RUN (size then 6 GB).
Fix 2: keep the dataset out of the image and supply it at run time through a read-only bind mount or volume, which also removes the 6 GB from the image entirely.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.
